label: Headphones ad, English
note: A plain ecommerce ad with about 14 reviewable claims, such as "#1 rated", "lifetime guarantee" and "better than Bose at half the price". A good scan flags most of them, so check that comparisons and "this weekend only" are on the list.

label: US supplement landing page
note: Supplement page that carries the standard FDA disclaimer. The disclaimer itself is required wording and should not be treated as a health claim, while claims like "boosts immunity" and "no side effects" should be.

label: Canadian loan and credit card offer
note: Lender copy with "pre-approved", "no credit check" and a 0% promo rate. Each of these needs a rate, term or condition next to it, so look for them in the results.

label: Ontario car dealer pricing
note: Dealer ad mixing "from" prices, monthly payments and "all-in pricing" with freight added later. Prices that leave out mandatory fees are a common compliance problem, so read this one by hand too.

label: UK and EU tour operator offer
note: Travel offer with scarcity lines ("only 2 rooms left"), a "from" price and a carbon neutral claim. Each of these needs proof or a full price to be safe.

label: Quebec ad in French
note: A French-language ad with about 16 claims. The scanner is built around English wording, so a short or empty result here does not mean the copy is clean.

label: French translation of the headphones ad
note: The same ad as the first example, translated. Compare the two results: the same claims should be found in both languages, so any gap shows what the scanner misses in French.

label: Health and savings claims in unusual wording
note: Real claims phrased in ways the scanner does not recognise. A low or green result does not mean the copy is safe, and each claim should still be reviewed.

label: Shorter version, no patterns matched
note: Six claims that are worded to slip past pattern matching. "No risky claim patterns found" would be the wrong takeaway, so read the copy yourself.

label: Plumbing catalogue, no real claims
note: Ordinary catalogue text with words like "Green Bay", "best practices" and "treat yourself". There are no real claims, so any red flags here are false alarms and should be dismissed.

label: Numbered list and stray qualifiers
note: A numbered list plus unrelated "terms apply" style wording. There is one real claim, and the asterisk has no footnote, so a message saying a footnote is present would be wrong.
